task.goal: Help adult learners recognize misleading averages in a short public-health chart.
hard_constraints: One 50-minute class with 12 learners and printed charts; no internet or personal medical data.
Learners must compare mean and median without assuming prior statistics training.
Check transfer to a new chart and time spent, not just recall of definitions.
task.available_resources: Whiteboard and two anonymized example datasets.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Move one value: make the misleading average visible
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: learners physically rearrange printed value slips to see how one unusually large observation moves the mean while leaving the median relatively stable. This makes sensitivity to extreme values tangible before introducing terminology.

Prepare a short public-health chart and 12 value slips derived from the first anonymized dataset, preserving a relevant extreme value if one exists. Explain mean as an equal share of the total and median as the middle of an ordered line; demonstrate the even-number case. Learners work in four groups of three, ordering slips and calculating both summaries with guided arithmetic. They then replace the largest value with a clearly labeled hypothetical larger value and predict which summary changes. Groups annotate the chart with what its average reveals and conceals. Explicitly explain that neither summary is automatically misleading: the appropriate choice depends on the question, distribution, and labeling.

Schedule: initial chart judgment, 4 minutes; common explanation, 8; assigned activity, 12; discussion, 8; individual transfer assessment, 10; feedback, 8. Keep the second dataset unseen until transfer. Its chart should use a different health measure and scale.

Needs: printed charts, slips, arithmetic scaffolds, whiteboard, and an instructor timepiece. Assumes the datasets contain manageable numerical observations. If neither has useful asymmetry, use a labeled hypothetical modification for instruction, while acknowledging that transfer to strongly skewed data remains untested. This lesson addresses distributional distortion, not every possible chart problem.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Randomly assign two groups to the manipulation activity and two to an equal-length worked example covering the same calculations. Before shared discussion, collect a brief independent explanation; treat the later transfer comparison cautiously because discussion may reduce differences. On the unseen chart, require each learner to calculate or locate mean and median, assess a headline, and explain which summary fits a stated question. Record completion time and unfinished responses at ten minutes. Score calculations and justified interpretation separately. The mechanism is weakened if manipulation produces no clearer explanation of extreme-value effects than the worked example, or only improves answers by requiring substantially more time. With 12 learners, results are descriptive.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Audit the headline against the question
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: teach learners to evaluate an average as evidence for a specific public-health claim. The central action is checking whether a summary answers the question being asked, rather than spotting an unusual number alone.

Use the first dataset to prepare one short chart with its underlying values and two possible headlines: one about a typical observation and one about the total divided across observations. Both must be plausible enough to inspect, without implying either mean or median is always preferable. In four groups of three, learners complete an audit sheet: What is being claimed? What does each observation represent? What is the mean? What is the median? Which headline is supported, and what qualification is needed? Rotate reader, calculator, and challenger roles. Groups then rewrite one headline so its summary and scope are explicit.

Schedule: individual first impression, 5 minutes; plain-language instruction in mean and median, 8; assigned practice, 12; individual transfer, 10; comparison of reasoning, 10; corrective feedback, 5. Introduce the second dataset only during transfer, with a new chart, headline, units, and practical question. Ask learners to accept, qualify, or reject the claim and support their decision numerically.

Needs: printed charts, audit sheets, arithmetic guides, whiteboard, and an instructor timepiece. Assumes the datasets have enough context to identify their observational units. Do not invent missing population or sampling information; mark those limits explicitly. This approach may improve claim evaluation while leaving independent calculation fragile, so both require assessment. Avoid teaching a shortcut that ‘typical’ always mandates the median.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Randomly assign six learners to the audit sheet and six to a conventional calculate-and-define worksheet using the same first dataset and equal practice time. Give everyone identical instruction and the same individual transfer chart before discussion. Score correct mean and median separately from whether the learner connects the chosen summary to the claim and acknowledges a relevant limitation. Record each learner’s completion time, with a ten-minute cap and unfinished work retained. Include one transfer question for which the mean is useful, so blanket rejection of means fails. The audit mechanism is challenged if learners merely repeat cautionary language, cannot justify decisions using the new values, or perform no better than the comparator on claim evaluation. Offer the audit sheet to everyone afterward.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Predict, inspect, and revise a distribution
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: expose the information lost in a single average by asking learners to predict the underlying observations, then compare their predictions with the actual distribution. A mismatch creates a concrete reason to inspect both mean and median.

Start with a printed public-health chart showing only the mean from the first dataset. Ask learners to sketch where they expect individual observations to lie on a supplied number line; stress that several distributions could fit. Reveal the actual anonymized values on a second printed panel. Learners compare their sketches with the observations, order the values, and find the median. Introduce mean as equal sharing and median as the middle position, with a worked example and support for even-sized datasets. In pairs, learners explain what the original chart allowed them to infer and what it left uncertain. They revise its caption or add a small distribution display.

Schedule: prediction, 5 minutes; explanation, 8; assigned inspection activity, 12; individual transfer, 10; discussion and revision, 10; feedback, 5. Use the second dataset for an unseen chart with different units. Its assessment asks learners to distinguish conclusions supported by the mean alone from conclusions requiring the displayed observations, then compare mean and median once the observations are revealed.

Needs: paired printed chart panels, number-line sheets, whiteboard, arithmetic supports, and an instructor timepiece. Assumes the source values are available and small enough to inspect on paper. Predictions are hypotheses, not errors to ridicule. The mechanism may be less striking when the first dataset is nearly symmetric; even then, multiple possible distributions remain a valid lesson.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Randomly assign three pairs to predict before seeing the values and three pairs to inspect the same values immediately. Keep numerical instruction, materials, and total practice time equal. Assess transfer individually before group discussion. Score whether learners avoid unsupported claims about most observations, correctly compare mean and median, and use the revealed distribution to justify a conclusion. Record time separately for the mean-only judgment and the subsequent full-data judgment, within the ten-minute assessment window. The prediction step is not supported if it adds time without improving calibrated conclusions relative to immediate inspection, or if learners become indiscriminately distrustful even after adequate data are shown. Treat this small comparison as a classroom feasibility check, not a reliable effect estimate.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Repair a plausible mistake before it becomes a rule
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: learners diagnose and repair incorrect worked solutions. Comparing a plausible error with a correct explanation could help them distinguish arithmetic mistakes from unsupported interpretations, and recognize those errors in a new chart. The active ingredient is explaining why a tempting solution fails.

Prepare a printed public-health chart and underlying observations from the first anonymized dataset. Add two clearly labeled fictional student solutions: one finds the median without ordering the values; another correctly calculates the mean but claims that most observations must equal or exceed it. Supply correct calculations separately for checking. Use actual dataset values; if the second claim happens to be true, explain that the mean alone still cannot establish it.

Use 5 minutes for an initial individual judgment, 8 for instruction, 12 for paired practice, 5 for individual explanation, 10 for unseen transfer, and 10 for discussion and feedback. Explain mean as total divided equally and median as the middle after ordering, including the two-middle-values case. During practice, six pairs identify the first unjustified step, repair it, and write a brief explanation that would help its fictional author. Emphasize that either summary can be useful, depending on the question.

Needs: printed charts, solution sheets, arithmetic guides, whiteboard, and an instructor timepiece. Reserve the second dataset for transfer. Its chart must include sufficient observations to compare both summaries. Missing sampling context remains explicitly unknown. Incorrect examples require prompt correction; learners with fragile arithmetic may otherwise remember the error.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Assign three pairs to error repair and three to correct worked examples with equivalent explanation prompts and equal practice time. Before discussion, assess everyone individually on the second chart without fictional solutions: calculate mean and median, evaluate a claim about most observations, and explain an appropriate use of each summary. Record completion times and unfinished work at ten minutes. Score calculations and justified interpretations separately. The mechanism lacks support if repair learners repeat the planted errors, cannot transfer without error labels, or show no interpretation advantage over correct examples despite taking longer. Twelve learners provide a feasibility check, not a reliable effect estimate.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Choose an average by seeing what a decision costs
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: learners compare the consequences of using the mean or median as a planning number. Equal-sharing and typical-observation questions become concrete through two different measures of success: matching the observed total and minimizing total absolute distance from individual observations. This could replace the shortcut “one average is always better” with an understanding of why the question matters.

Use the first anonymized dataset and its public-health chart. Explain mean as total divided by count and median as the middle after ordering, including the even-count case. In four groups of three, learners calculate both using printed arithmetic guides. They then complete two paper challenges: multiply each proposed average by the observation count and compare with the actual total; calculate each observation’s distance from each proposed average and add those distances. Explain that distance means the positive gap, without introducing formal notation. The mean reproduces the total; the median minimizes total absolute distance, although ties are possible.

Groups annotate the chart with one question each summary helps answer and one conclusion the chart cannot establish. Clarify that minimizing numerical distance does not establish the best public-health policy, and a median need not be an observed value.

Schedule: initial chart judgment, 4 minutes; instruction, 9; challenges, 14; individual unseen-chart assessment, 10; discussion and feedback, 13.

Needs: printed charts, calculation tables, whiteboard, and an instructor timepiece. Reserve the second dataset for transfer. Assumes manageable numerical values with meaningful totals and differences; inspect this before teaching. Do not relabel observations or invent sampling context. If mean and median coincide, the exercise demonstrates agreement but provides weaker evidence about recognizing misleading averages.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Give two groups the consequence challenges and two an equal-duration calculation worksheet with the same instruction. Before shared feedback, assess all 12 learners individually on the second chart: calculate mean and median, select a summary for each of two stated purposes, and judge a claim about typical observations using the displayed values. Record completion minutes and unfinished items at the ten-minute cap. Score arithmetic separately from justified interpretation. The mechanism is challenged if learners can complete the distance table but cannot select and justify summaries on transfer, or gain no interpretive advantage while taking longer. This small comparison assesses feasibility, not a dependable causal effect.

EXPAND.title: Count the observations behind each average
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: make unequal group sizes visible so learners stop treating an average of group averages as the average of all observations. This addresses a misleading-average error that can survive correct definitions of mean and median.

Before class, the instructor checks whether the first anonymized dataset can be printed as a manageable list of observations. Divide that list into two unequal batches, explicitly labeled as teaching partitions rather than real demographic groups. Prepare a chart displaying each batch’s mean and count, plus a headline claiming an overall mean obtained by averaging the two batch means equally. Use this claim only if it actually differs from the pooled mean. If no useful difference occurs, this route is unsuitable for the supplied data.

Schedule: initial judgment, 4 minutes; explain mean as equal sharing and median as the middle ordered observation, including even counts, 8; practice, 14; individual transfer, 10; discussion, 9; correction, 5. In four groups of three, learners reconstruct the combined total and count, calculate the pooled mean and median, and repair the headline. Show that subgroup medians also cannot generally be averaged to obtain the pooled median.

Reserve the second dataset for an unfamiliar chart with different units and unequal teaching partitions. Ask learners to compare pooled mean and median, inspect an overall-average claim, and explain what additional information would be needed if only subgroup summaries were available.

Needs: printed charts, underlying values, calculation guides, whiteboard, and an instructor timepiece. Arithmetic must be manageable without calculators. The lesson supports conclusions about the displayed observations; artificial partitions do not support claims about actual health subgroups.
EXPAND.experiment: The instructor owns one 50-minute trial. Randomly assign six learners to the count-reconstruction practice and six to an equal-duration headline-audit worksheet using the same data and numerical instruction. Assess everyone individually before discussion. Score pooled-mean accuracy, median accuracy, and justified claim evaluation separately; record completion times and unfinished responses at ten minutes. Also count incorrect attempts to average subgroup medians, a possible shifted risk. Stop developing this route if the data cannot produce an honest, accessible example. Do not prefer it over headline auditing unless transfer judgments improve without more unfinished work or more median-aggregation errors. With 12 learners, findings are descriptive.

EXPAND.title: Remove the calculation bottleneck with an error-checking scaffold
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: externalize the steps most likely to overload a novice’s working memory, allowing attention to reach interpretation. Learners can understand an average’s limitation yet fail to recognize it on a new chart because sorting, counting, and division consume their attention.

Prepare the first dataset beside its short public-health chart. Provide a paper worksheet with numbered observation slots, a running-total column, a count box, and paired boxes marking the middle positions. Include two checks: the mean must lie between the smallest and largest observations, and the median must have at least half the observations on either side, counting ties appropriately. These checks catch some errors, not all.

Schedule: initial chart judgment, 4 minutes; plain-language demonstration of mean and median, 8; supported practice, 12; partial-scaffold practice, 6; individual transfer, 10; feedback and corrections, 10. Learners work in four groups of three, then repeat the interpretation individually with fewer prompts. They must explain whether a chart’s average supports a supplied statement about the observations, using both summaries and the actual values. Neither summary is taught as universally preferable.

Keep the second dataset unseen until transfer. Print its chart with different units and underlying observations, plus a blank optional scaffold. Require calculation of both summaries and a qualified headline judgment. Learners mark whether they used the scaffold; independent recognition does not require unsupported mental arithmetic.

Needs: printed charts and worksheets, whiteboard, and an instructor timepiece. This route assumes short numerical lists and usable contextual labels. It cannot resolve missing population information. If arithmetic becomes a barrier during feedback, provide verified summaries and revisit interpretation, while recording that calculation remained unsupported.
EXPAND.experiment: The instructor runs one class with six learners randomly assigned to scaffolded practice and six to the prior headline-audit approach with ordinary working space. Match instruction and practice duration. Give everyone the same optional blank scaffold at transfer. Record calculation errors, interpretation scores, completion time, and unfinished work. Inspect whether learners can explain the result without merely pointing to worksheet boxes; dependence on prompts is the principal shifted risk. The scaffold offers no improvement if it saves calculation time but leaves claim evaluation unchanged, or improves accuracy only by increasing unfinished interpretations. Stop extending the worksheet after this trial unless it improves transfer within the ten-minute cap. Report descriptive learner counts, not a reliable causal effect.

EXPAND.title: Teach a decision boundary: conclude, qualify, or request information
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: practice deciding when the displayed evidence permits interpretation and when a missing summary or distribution requires an information request. Recognition becomes a usable action rule rather than generalized suspicion of averages.

The instructor prepares versions of the first dataset’s chart with different amounts of information. Teach mean as equal sharing and median as the middle ordered observation, with a short calculation of each. Then introduce a narrow decision rule: a labeled mean can support a statement about the total divided by the observation count; a claim about what most observations experience requires evidence about their distribution. A median alone does not establish every claim about a majority.

Schedule: first impression, 4 minutes; numerical instruction, 8; decision demonstration, 8; paired practice, 12; individual transfer, 10; feedback and recovery, 8. Use six pairs. Practice includes a close pair: the same claim about how many observations exceed a threshold, first with only a mean and then with the full values. Learners either request the missing distribution or count directly and decide. Their request must identify the missing information and explain its purpose. Reveal the values on paper so they can recover from an initial wrong choice.

Reserve the second dataset for one unfamiliar transfer chart, accompanied by its values in a folded panel. Learners record an initial action, request or reveal information if needed, compare mean and median, and give a final judgment.

Needs: printed panels, decision sheets, whiteboard, and an instructor timepiece. The handoff is a simulated request to the chart’s author, not medical advice. Missing sampling context remains an explicit limit even after the values are revealed.
EXPAND.experiment: The instructor owns one bounded trial, randomly assigning six learners to decision-boundary practice and six to equal-duration headline auditing. Both groups receive identical mean-and-median instruction and the same individual assessment: a close pair on opposite sides of the information boundary and the unfamiliar second-dataset chart. Score action choice, specificity of the request, numerical comparison, and final judgment. Record total time, unnecessary information requests, and unsupported conclusions. These expose the shifted risk of teaching excessive hesitation. Stop revising this route if it produces no more correct final judgments than headline auditing, or if extra requests cause more ten-minute timeouts. With 12 learners, use the results to inspect feasibility and errors rather than claim effectiveness.

EXPAND.title: Retrieve the method after the cues disappear
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: require learners to retrieve and apply the comparison after a short interruption, then correct errors immediately. This targets dependence on recently visible instructions: learners may succeed beside a worked example but fail when a new chart no longer cues the procedure.

Prepare a short public-health chart and the first anonymized dataset, one worked example, two practice sheets, and a correction key. Explain mean as equal sharing and median as the middle ordered value, including an even-sized list. Explicitly connect a large mean–median difference with a reason to inspect the values, while explaining that a small difference does not establish that a chart’s claim is sound.

Schedule: initial judgment, 4 minutes; instruction and worked example, 8; guided practice, 8; unrelated-to-calculation chart-reading task, 4; closed-example retrieval and correction, 8; individual transfer, 10; feedback, 8. During the interruption, learners identify units, observation labels, and chart titles. Then cover the example and ask them to reconstruct the calculation steps and interpret the first chart from a fresh copy. Reveal the key, have learners locate one error or confirm their steps, and require a corrected explanation. Do not display a mnemonic during transfer.

Use the unseen second dataset for a chart with different units and a new claim. Learners calculate and compare mean and median, decide whether the claim is supported, and identify a relevant limitation. Collect responses before final discussion.

Needs: printed charts, cover sheets, correction keys, whiteboard, and an instructor timepiece. Values must allow hand calculation. This class can test immediate transfer after retrieval practice; it cannot establish durable retention without a later assessment.
EXPAND.experiment: The instructor runs one trial with six learners randomly assigned to retrieval-and-correction practice and six to an equal-duration open-example headline audit. Both conditions receive the same numerical instruction, chart-reading interruption, and unseen assessment. Score interpretation and calculation separately, recording individual completion times and unfinished responses at ten minutes. Inspect copied or confidently repeated calculation errors as a possible cost of unsuccessful retrieval. Prefer retrieval only if it improves justified transfer without increasing those errors or unfinished work. Stop adding retrieval rounds after this single trial if performance is no better than the audit comparator after accounting for time. Any apparent advantage remains descriptive and says nothing yet about long-term retention.

EXPAND.title: Substantive upgrade: Audit the headline, with timed transfer and calculation recovery
EXPAND.proposal:
Source: “Audit the headline against the question.” This is the strongest currently usable route because its main action directly matches the goal: judge whether an average supports a public-health claim. Preserve its claim audit, rotating group roles, headline repair, unseen transfer chart, and caution that neither mean nor median is universally preferable. The changed action is to collect individual completion times and preserve an interpretation check when arithmetic stalls. The source requests numerical justification but does not specify how to measure time or distinguish calculation difficulty from failure to recognize a misleading claim.

Mechanism: learners connect a headline to its observational unit, numerical summary, and intended question. Mean means adding all values and dividing by their count; median means ordering values and finding the middle, averaging the two middle values for an even count. A difference between them prompts inspection of the observations; it does not by itself prove deception.

Preparation: the instructor checks both anonymized datasets, calculates answer keys, and prints short charts with underlying values and units. Use the first dataset for practice and reserve the second for transfer. Prepare two claims for practice: one about total divided across observations and one about a typical observation. Claims must be judged against the actual data; do not force a misleading example if the values do not support one. Any instructional alteration must be labeled hypothetical. Do not invent sampling or population context.

Run one 50-minute class for 12 learners: individual first impression, 5 minutes; plain-language instruction and worked calculations, 8; practice in four groups of three, 12; individual transfer, 10; comparison of reasoning, 10; corrective feedback, 5. During practice, rotate reader, calculator, and challenger. Each group identifies the claim and observational unit, calculates and compares mean and median, accepts, qualifies, or rejects the claim, and writes a more precise headline.

Transfer uses a new chart, units, and claim from the second dataset. Learners independently calculate both summaries, explain their difference, judge the headline using the observations, and state one relevant limit. The instructor announces elapsed minutes; learners mark when they finish, and unfinished work is recorded at the ten-minute cutoff. At minute six, collect or have learners cover their initial answers, then give everyone a separate sheet with verified summaries. Learners may complete or revise their interpretation in another ink or clearly labeled box. Preserve both responses: success after receiving summaries is supported interpretation, not independent calculation success.

Assessment: score mean calculation, median calculation, comparison, evidence-based headline judgment, and defensible rewrite separately. Record initial and final completion time, unfinished work, and whether verified summaries enabled recovery. Do not score definition recall as transfer.

Needs and limits: printed charts, worksheets, answer sheets, whiteboard, and an instructor clock; arithmetic must be manageable by hand. Preparation and the staged summary handout add modest instructor work. The instructor owns feedback and correction. Stop calculation at the scheduled cutoff, explain errors with the verified key, and mark unresolved interpretation for further teaching rather than inferring medical understanding. If contextual information is missing, learners should qualify the claim and identify what the chart author would need to supply. This class can assess immediate transfer, not lasting retention.
EXPAND.experiment:
In one 12-learner pilot, compare the upgrade with the source audit lesson as the practical alternative. Give all learners identical instruction and group practice. Randomly assign six transfer sheets to include the minute-six verified-summary recovery step and six to retain the source's calculation-and-judgment task throughout. Record elapsed completion time for everyone and score initial versus final answers separately. After collecting assessments, give everyone the verified summaries and full feedback within the scheduled class.

Inspect correct numerical comparisons, justified headline judgments, unfinished responses, and instructor time spent preparing and distributing the recovery sheets. The proposed benefit is better completion of valid interpretation when arithmetic blocks progress. Evidence against adopting the change would include no improvement in justified judgments, increased copying without supporting explanations, or disruption that displaces discussion. With six learners per condition, treat differences as feasibility signals, not evidence of reliable superiority. Retain the source lesson if the added handoff costs more class time than the useful recovery it enables.
